newsitem.title: USA: USDA accepts 16.1 mln acres for CRP --documents.
newsitem.headline: USDA accepts 16.1 mln acres for CRP --documents.

text.p: The Agriculture Department, living up to its promise of a speedy decision, accepted 16.1 million acres of U.S. cropland for entry into the long-term Conservation Reserve this fall, USDA documents said Thursday.

Contracts on 21.5 million acres expire on September 30, so 5.4 million acres would be freed for grain production or livestock grazing. This fall would see the largest turnover of land since the Conservation Reserve was created in 1985.
Documents prepared for a CRP briefing later Thursday said 16.1 million acres were accepted. Of the total, 11.7 million acres were re-enrolled from expiring contracts.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman says another "sign up" for the Conservation Reserve Program will be held this fall.

During a signup in March, farmers offered 25.6 million acres for the reserve, which pays farmers an annual rent to idle fragile land for 10 years. Goals of the reserve were reducing soil erosion, protecting water purity and improving wildlife habitat.
USDA sifted the offers, deciding which to accept, with a formula that considered the rent requested for a parcel and the environmental benefits that would be gained.
Slightly more than half of the expiring acreage was in seven, predominantly wheat-growing, states -- Colorado, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, North Dakota and Texas.
